title: Collections: lists
summary: Keep many values in order, change them in place, and know when two names share one list.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Build and change lists with methods, and know when two names share one list and when you have a copy.
analogy: A list is a shared shopping list on the fridge: anyone holding the same list sees every change, but a photocopy is separate.

misconceptions.belief: `b = a` makes a copy of the list.
misconceptions.correction: Both names refer to the same list; use `a.copy()` or `list(a)` for a copy.
It changes the list in place and returns None.

misconceptions.belief: Removing items while looping over the same list is safe.
misconceptions.correction: It skips items; loop over a copy, or build a new list.

rubric.evidence: functions that should change a list change it; others leave it alone
a new list is returned instead of an alias when the original must survive
append, insert, remove, pop and index are used correctly

review.recall: After `b = a` and `b.append(1)`, what is `a`? How do you make a real copy?

steps.title: Many values, one name
steps.body:
A week of temperatures, the songs in a playlist, the scores in a game: often you have many values that
belong together, in order. Giving each its own name (`temp1`, `temp2`, ...) doesn't scale. A **list**
holds them all under one name, and a loop can work through every one.

steps.title: Slots you can change, and shared lists
steps.body:
A list is like a string's row of numbered boxes, with one big difference: the boxes are **open**. You
can replace an item, add items to the end, or take items out, and it is still the *same* list.

That makes names matter more. A name is a label attached to a list. `b = a` doesn't copy anything:
it attaches a second label to the **same** list. Change the list through either name and both see
the change. Functions work the same way: a function given a list can change the caller's list.

questions: After `b = a` and `b.append(1)`, how many lists exist?
Why can a function change a list it was given, but not a string?

steps.title: Watch a function change the caller's list
steps.body: Watch `scores` and `mine`: two names, one list.

visual.code:
def add_bonus(scores):
    scores.append(10)

mine = [7, 9]
add_bonus(mine)
print(mine)

frames.note: A new list is created and the name `mine` is attached to it.
The parameter `scores` is attached to the very same list. Nothing is copied.
The call is over, but the change stays: `mine` was never a separate copy.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Create:** `[]` is empty; `[3, "hi", 2.5]` may mix types. `len`, indexing, negative indexes,
slicing, `in` and `for` loops all work exactly as with strings.

**Change in place:** `lst[i] = x` replaces an item. `lst.append(x)` adds to the end,
`lst.insert(i, x)` adds at position `i`, `lst.pop()` removes and returns the last item,
`lst.remove(x)` removes the first `x`, and `lst.sort()` sorts. All of these change the list in place.
`append`, `insert`, `remove` and `sort` return `None`, so `lst = lst.sort()` loses your list;
`pop` is the exception and returns the item it removed.

**Aliasing:** `b = a` makes a second name for the same list. A slice makes a **new** list, so
`b = a[:]` (or `list(a)`) is a copy. A list passed to a function is the caller's list; to leave the
caller's list alone, build and return a new one.

steps.title: Run it: a week of temperatures
steps.body: Predict the last line carefully before you press **Run**.
steps.code:
temps = [18, 21, 17, 24]
temps.append(20)
temps.sort()
print(temps)
print(temps[0], temps[-1])
backup = temps
backup.append(99)
print(temps)

steps.title: Your turn: keep the even numbers
steps.body:
Complete `evens(numbers)` so it returns a **new** list containing only the even numbers, in their
original order. The list you were given must not change.
hints: Start with an empty list, `result = []`, and return it at the end.

tests.name: keeps original order
tests.code: assert evens([4, 1, 2, 3, 0]) == [4, 2, 0], f'evens([4, 1, 2, 3, 0]) returned {evens([4, 1, 2, 3, 0])!r}; keep the original order'

tests.name: input unchanged
tests.code:
_data = [4, 1, 2, 3, 0]
_out = evens(_data)
assert _data == [4, 1, 2, 3, 0], f'the input was changed to {_data!r}; build a new list instead'
assert _out is not _data, 'return a new list, not the one you were given'

steps.title: Challenge: remove duplicates
steps.body:
Write `remove_duplicates(items)` that returns a new list with each item kept only the **first** time it
appears, in the original order: `[3, 1, 3, 2, 1]` becomes `[3, 1, 2]`. Don't change `items`.
hints: The starter copies everything. Before appending `x`, ask whether it is already in `result`.
`x not in result` is True when `x` hasn't been kept yet.

tests.name: empty
tests.code: assert remove_duplicates([]) == [], 'an empty list stays empty'

tests.name: already unique: still a new list
tests.code:
_data = [1, 2]
_out = remove_duplicates(_data)
assert _out == [1, 2] and _out is not _data, 'return a new list even when there is nothing to remove'

tests.name: input unchanged
tests.code:
_data = [1, 1]
remove_duplicates(_data)
assert _data == [1, 1], f'the input was changed to {_data!r}'

steps.title: Transfer: a playlist
hints: Copy first: `result = songs.copy()`, then `result.remove(title)` and `result.insert(0, title)` if it is present.
In `add_unique`, `if title not in songs: songs.append(title)`.

tests.name: returns a new list and leaves the original alone
tests.code:
songs = ['a', 'b']
out = move_to_front(songs, 'b')
assert songs == ['a', 'b'], 'move_to_front changed the original list'
assert out is not songs, 'return a new list, not the same one'
missing = move_to_front(songs, 'z')
assert missing == songs and missing is not songs, 'when the title is missing, return a copy'

tests.name: add_unique changes the list in place
tests.code:
songs = ['a']
same = songs
assert add_unique(songs, 'b') is None
assert same == ['a', 'b'], 'add_unique should change the list itself'

tests.name: add_unique returns nothing either way
tests.code: assert add_unique(['a'], 'a') is None and add_unique(['a'], 'b') is None

steps.title: Check your understanding
steps.body: Trace each one in your head first.

questions.explanation: `y = x` makes a second name for the same list, so appending through `y` changes `x` too.
`sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`; `sorted(...)` would return a new list.
`a[:]` is a slice, which is a new list, so `b` is a separate copy.
A slice from position 1 to the end.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Create lists, read items by position, and loop over them.
- Change a list in place with assignment and methods, remembering that most of them return `None`
  (`pop` returns the removed item).
- Predict when two names share one list, and make a real copy with a slice when you need one.
- Write functions that build and return new lists instead of changing their input.

Next: dictionaries, which find values by a **key** instead of by position.
